title: Short Stuff: Boba Tea
summary: Josh and Chuck's Short Stuff episode on boba tea (bubble tea). They open with banter wishing Dave well after back surgery and discuss their tastes for boba. They cover the origin of boba tea in Taiwan in the 1980s, with two rival tea shops (Hanlin Tea Room in Tainan, founder Tsung-Ho Tsai, and Chun Shui Tang, with Lin Hsiu-hui) each claiming credit; the 1940s bartender Chang Fan Chu and the milk tea and frothy shaken-tea lineage; spread to the US West Coast in the 1990s and mainstream in the 2000s. They explain that "boba" is Taiwanese slang for breast, that tapioca is starch from cassava, made into pearls from rice or palm hearts historically, how to cook tapioca pearls, the Chinese term "QQ" for perfect chewiness, and unusual toppings like salted cheese foam. They close with a suggestion to try a taro or dirty taro drink with and without boba, and the iHeartRadio production credit.

segments.title: Opening banter and boba preferences
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode, wish Dave well after back surgery, and talk about their feelings toward boba, with Josh disliking the chewy texture and suggesting ordering it without the boba.

segments.title: What boba tea is
segments.summary: Chuck describes boba tea, also called bubble tea, as a Taiwanese tea with tapioca pearls in it.

segments.title: Competing origin stories from Taiwan in the 1980s
segments.summary: Two rival Taiwanese tea shops each claim to have invented boba tea. Hanlin Tea Room in Tainan says founder Tsung-Ho Tsai added tapioca balls to milk tea in 1986. Chun Shui Tang says a 20-year-old worker, Lin Hsiu-hui, added tapioca pudding to her tea in 1987.

segments.title: Milk tea history and spread to the US
segments.summary: Milk tea predates boba by decades; a 1940s bartender, Chang Fan Chu, shook teas with milk that frothed. Boba tea reached the US West Coast in the 1990s and became popular with hipsters in the 2000s. Modern variations include non-dairy milks and toppings.

segments.title: Meaning of the word boba
segments.summary: Josh explains that boba is Taiwanese slang for breast, which is why the drink's pearls get a playful name.

segments.title: Tapioca, cassava, and making tapioca pearls
segments.summary: Tapioca is starch from cassava root, which grows well in Southeast Asia. Early pearls were made from rice or palm hearts. Chuck describes boiling dry pearls for about thirty minutes and then cooling them, and the hosts note how the texture is easy to get wrong.

segments.title: Texture, QQ, and unusual toppings
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the chewy texture of boba, compare it to gummy bears, and say the Chinese term QQ describes the perfect chewiness. They mention a salted cheese foam topping reported by the Seattle Times.

segments.title: Ordering suggestions
segments.summary: Josh suggests trying a taro or dirty taro drink, with and without boba, and Chuck says he will try it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode and give the iHeartRadio production credit.
